text.p: The announced resignation from parliament today of one of Australia's most notable backbenchers, John Langmore, will produce the second by-election of the Howard government, this time in Canberra.

But don't expect a rerun of the Lindsay fiasco, the October by-election where Labor was thrashed in one of its traditionally safe seats as the previously disqualified Liberal candidate stormed back with a breathtaking increased majority.

Without polling to work on, Canberra Watch would be surprised if Labor could now lose a seat in our national capital. The Liberals might not even run a candidate when the by-election is held early next year, especially since the seat might be abolished in the next general election.

Canberra is not like the rest of Australia (in case anyone needed telling). When the Federal government feels a need to crack down on public spending, the national interest is exactly the reverse of Canberra's.
The nation may cheer the government on -- and judging from Lindsay and the polls, that is exactly what it is doing -- but Canberra will sulk.

At the moment, the only thing that's booming in our national capital seems to be restaurants. One cannot pop out for a curry these days without sitting next to a large table of public servants farewelling someone who's taken a redundancy package.
Property values are down and the Australian Capital Territory unemployment rate is now, for the first time in memory, about the same as the national rate.

Riding on the cushion of public funding, the territory unemployment rate has always been below the national rate -- well below during recessions. Its interest coincides with lots of public spending and it tends to vote Labor almost as strongly as Newcastle, although for rather different reasons.
Canberra has recanted its 1995 sin of voting in Liberal candidate Brendan Smyth, whose by-election victory was, in retrospect, one of the biggest signals that Paul Keating was a goner.
Too late, Canberra realised with horror what was in store for it, and Smyth's was the only scalp that Labor claimed in the 1996 election.

One reason why the Liberals might not run a candidate in the by-election is that one Canberra seat will probably be abolished in 1999, so the junior MP who replaces Langmore will probably get just two years in parliament.

Canberra had only two Federal seats until 1993, when a third was added. However, even before the public spending cuts it was clear that Canberra was not keeping up with national population growth, leaving it with a little less than the 2.5 quotas of people needed to justify the third seat.
Even the potential Labor candidates are wondering whether it's worth standing.
